newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian housing shows some signs of stalling.
newsitem.headline: Australian housing shows some signs of stalling.

text.p: Australia's housing recovery has slowed after a strong start to the year, with March data released on Monday showing a second successive fall that left approvals showing negative growth over the March quarter.
Housing finance fell 1.3 percent in March, under median forecasts of a 1.0 percent rise and at the bottom end of the range of forecasts, official data showed.
While the data has raised some questions over the strength of the expected recovery, economists said fundamentals remained supportive of the housing sector.
Housing is expected to be one of the key drivers of the expected strengthening through 1997, but after a strong start to the year the figures have shown some softness.
After rising five percent in both December and January, total housing finance approvals have fallen in the past two months, and were down 3.6 percent over the March quarter.
"Overall, the data shows housing finance stalling after a strong start to the year," HSBC Markets economist Anthony Thompson said.
In the figures one area of concern is that new housing approvals have softened.
Both approvals for the construction of dwellings and the purchase of newly erected dwellings are below their December 1996 level.

The reason this is concerning, especially the softness in contruction, is that it is the flow-through effects from new housing to employment, manufacturing and retail demand that are expected to drive the stronger economy later this year.
"It doesn't look like an economy to me that's rocketing away," Dresdner Australia chief economist Rob Henderson said.
"Is this just like a pause after a very solid start to 1997, or is it actually something a liitle bit deeper?" he asked, adding he was not sure of the answer.

But despite the weakness, economists said the conditions were still favourable for an housing upturn, pointing to improved affordability and a rundown with mortgage rates at their lowest levels for 25 years, a lift in the households savings rate and improving consumer spending.

"It seems to me that most of the oversupply of housing has been cleared now, you've still got population growth which is going to drive housing demand higher, and in a fundamental sense affordability is really going to kick in," Noumra senior economist Andrew Pease said.
"You can't have interest rates as low as they are without starting some sort of housing interest," he said.
A combination of three official rate cuts in the second half of 1996 and competition-inspired cuts have seen mortgage rates fall to their lowest level in 25 years.
The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) remains optimistic on housing, saying last week that the lower rates should be supportive of housing.
"Forward indicators of housing activity are continuing to point to an upswing in that sector," the RBA said in its semi-annual statement on monetary policy released last week.
